## Please read the syllabus!

This page has important information about the course, including its structure, assignments, grading, and student hours, [among many others](https://phdcomics.com/comics.php?f=1583).

<b><a href="https://www.cameo.com/v/5f2b392a0299b100202e624a?utm_campaign=video_share_to_copy" style="color: #981e32">Even Snoop Dogg wants you to read the syllabus!</a></b>

:::


## Course objectives

This course provides an introduction to statistics in education research. You will acquire essential tools that allow you to read, interpret, and draw conclusions from quantitative education research.

In this course, you will learn how to

- describe and define key concepts related to education research,
- read and explain key statistical concepts found in education research studies, and
- perform statistical calculations related to education research.

We build intuition first. You will run simulations, work with real data from a study of students in India, and keep asking one question: is this number the truth about everyone (a *parameter*), or only our *estimate* of it from a sample?

### Expectations

In this course, you will be expected to

- come to our lectures on Tuesdays and Thursdays,
- attend your own lab every Friday,
- do the readings before class,
- complete the Mastery Training and Problem Sets in MindTap,
- take two short checks and three quizzes in the Friday labs,
- take two in-person exams, and
- complete the course evaluation.

### Connections to other classes

[EDUC 10](https://catalogue.uci.edu/search/?P=EDUC%2010) (Educational Research Design) is a prerequisite for this course. Beyond that, the course makes no assumptions about prior knowledge of statistics, apart from basic math skills. Not sure about your math? Try the Math Skills Assessment in Appendix A of our book.

[EDUC 157](https://catalogue.uci.edu/search/?P=EDUC%20157) (Educational Research and Evaluation) and [EDUC 159](https://catalogue.uci.edu/search/?P=EDUC%20159) (Experimental Research Methods) build on EDUC 10 and EDUC 15.

### My promise

I *promise* you can succeed in this course.

This course is all about practical application. You will notice "How will I ever use this?" is a question I consider for every class.

Now, you will have to tool up. You will hear about weird new concepts, use some unfamiliar math, learn new software, and approach practical questions from a new perspective. Initially, some of this might pose challenges. Most everything will be new to you. But, it's perfectly normal not to grasp concepts immediately and make mistakes during your initial encounters. This is how you acquire new skills and build a strong toolkit.

Many parallels come to mind. Learning to ride a bike. Learning a new language. Learning how to use a hammer (and when to pick a different tool). Building muscle through training. All of these demand time, grit, and—oftentimes—productive failure. All of them are easier with friends, through apprenticeship, consistency, and by working with a coach. Similarly, if you find yourself struggling with some of the course content, that's a *good* sign. When you do, take a breather, talk to classmates, ask questions, or contact our teaching team for assistance.

## Course structure

This syllabus reflects a plan for the quarter. Deviations may become necessary as the quarter progresses.

### Flow of the course

The course follows the same routine every week.

- **Before class**: Do the reading for the topic.
- **Tuesday and Thursday**: Lecture, 12:30–1:50 PM in EDUC 2009. Each class runs about 20 minutes of talk, then a few minutes where you do something (predict, try, or play), three times over. None of it is scored.
- **Friday**: Lab with {{< var assistant.name_no_title >}}, at 12:00 PM (Lab A1, EDUC 2009) or 1:00 PM (Lab A2, EDUC 2001). Go to the lab you're enrolled in.
- **Sunday, 6 PM**: The week's Mastery Training and Problem Set are due in MindTap, with an automatic one-day extension (see [Late assignments](#late-assignments)).

You can find every class, lab, and due date on the [schedule page](/schedule.qmd).

### Labs

Seven of our ten Friday labs follow one routine. You solve a by-hand, exam-style problem in pairs, then work on the same idea with real data in a spreadsheet or the [course simulator](/resource/simulator.qmd), and finally write one sentence on what the result means and hand it in. Each lab comes with a one-page handout on this website. Labs 2 and 8 start with a 15-minute individual check.

The other three labs (Labs 3, 6, and 10) are quiz days. Labs 6 and 10 also review for the exams. We'll explain the format in class.

If you can, bring a laptop to lab. You'll work in pairs, so one laptop per pair is enough.

### This website and Canvas

This website holds the syllabus, the schedule, a page for each topic with its slides, the lab handouts, and other resources.

Our Canvas page is [here]({{< var course.canvas >}}). We use Canvas for

1. **MindTap**: the ebook, Mastery Training, and Problem Sets all open through Canvas.
2. **Grades**: I post your grades on Canvas.
3. **Solutions and slides**: solutions to the lab problems, and my slides as HTML (accessible version) and PDF (for printing).

Please update your Canvas settings and notifications to make sure you receive announcements. Click on ["settings"](https://canvas.eee.uci.edu/profile/settings) to add another email address and/or a cell phone number to receive notifications. Click on ["notifications"](https://canvas.eee.uci.edu/profile/communication) to configure how you receive Canvas notifications.

## Course materials

### Book and MindTap

Frederick J. Gravetter, Larry B. Wallnau, Lori-Ann B. Forzano, and James E. Witnauer, *Essentials of Statistics for the Behavioral Sciences*, 10th ed. (Cengage, 2021).

We use the book through Cengage MindTap, which includes the ebook and the homework. MindTap works only through our Canvas page, so start there. I'll post how to get access, and the price for our course, on Canvas before the quarter begins.

If the cost of MindTap is a problem for you, please email me. Don't let it keep you from starting the homework.

### Spreadsheets and the simulator

You'll use Google Sheets or Excel, whichever you prefer. We only use functions that work in both, such as `AVERAGE`, `STDEV.S`, and `CORREL`. You do not need R or any other programming language. I'll show you some R output on the slides, and you'll learn to read it.

You'll also use our [course simulator](/resource/simulator.qmd) in class and in labs. It runs in your browser, and it's based on [Kristoffer Magnusson](https://rpsychologist.com/)'s visualizations.

### Calculator

Please bring a calculator to labs and exams. A basic scientific calculator is enough.

## Assignments and grades

### Quizzes

There are five scored events in our Friday labs: a 15-minute individual check in each of Labs 2 and 8, and a quiz in each of Labs 3, 6, and 10. Each is worth 10 points. I'll count your best four. Go to your own lab for each of them.

### Labs

Each lab is worth 3 points. In a regular lab, you earn them by being there and handing in a real attempt at the sentence, which doesn't have to be correct. On a quiz day, you earn them by being there. I'll count your best seven of the ten labs.

### Mastery Training and Problem Sets

You'll complete two types of homework in MindTap, for Chapters 5 to 12 and 14. Both are due on Sundays at 6 PM, with an automatic one-day extension (see [Late assignments](#late-assignments)). There are nine of each, worth 5 points each, and I'll count your best eight of each type. Chapters 1 to 4 have the same two activities as ungraded practice, open all quarter.

The **Mastery Training** helps you become familiar with the important terms and ideas in each chapter. You have unlimited attempts.

The **Problem Sets** strengthen your knowledge of the concepts and procedures covered in each chapter. You have three attempts, and I keep your highest score. A score of at least 75% earns full credit (5 points), and a score below 75% earns no credit.

MindTap is your practice. The by-hand problems in the Friday labs are what look most like the exams.

### Exams

There are two in-person exams, each worth 100 points.

- The **midterm exam** takes place in class on Tuesday, February 16 (Week 7). It covers Chapters 1 to 9 and takes 80 minutes. We review in class on Thursday, February 11, and in Lab 6 on Friday, February 12.
- The **final exam** is cumulative. It takes place during finals week, on the date the Registrar sets.

Both exams are free response and built on the data we use in class. They test your intuition as well as your calculations: for example, whether a number is a parameter or an estimate.

The exams are open book: you can bring any print materials you like, including your own notes and cheat sheets. You must not use any electronic devices, except a calculator (and anything permitted by an accommodation you may have). We also attach the z, t, and F tables and a formula sheet to each exam.

If you'd prefer to take an exam in a language other than English, I can provide a translated version, in any language. Just email me. I'll announce the date to ask by in class.

### Course evaluation

You earn 9 points for completing the course evaluation at the end of the quarter.

Personally, I like the plus-delta approach. Start by telling me what you like. These are things I should maintain and build on. Then, provide opportunities for improvements. These should be action-oriented suggestions as to how I can provide a more effective course. This feedback is very important to me, and I appreciate your input.

### Grading

You (the student) and I (the instructor) should care the most about what you *learn*, not what numerical/letter summary of that learning you get at the end of the quarter. So I would love to not have grades at all, but unfortunately we humans are very good at procrastinating on our good intentions when there is no incentive not to. Thus, we have grades to help solve this commitment problem and to encourage you to put effort into learning the course material.

Here is how each part of the course contributes to your overall grade.

| Category          | Points | How it counts                              |
|:------------------|-------:|:-------------------------------------------|
| Quizzes           |     40 | Best 4 of 5 Friday events, 10 points each  |
| Labs              |     21 | Best 7 of 10 labs, 3 points each           |
| Mastery Training  |     40 | Best 8 of 9, 5 points each                 |
| Problem Sets      |     40 | Best 8 of 9, 5 points each                 |
| Midterm exam      |    100 | In person                                  |
| Final exam        |    100 | In person, cumulative                      |
| Course evaluation |      9 | For completing it                          |
| **Total**         | **350**|                                            |

You earn 261 of the 350 points in person: in the Friday labs and on the exams. Attendance at lectures isn't graded, but please come to every class.

:::{.callout-note}
## Grace policy

When calculating your grade, I drop your lowest quiz, your three lowest labs, your lowest Mastery Training, and your lowest Problem Set. Thus, if you have an emergency that forces you to miss a lab or a deadline, your grade will not be affected. The exams cannot be dropped.

:::

All grades will be posted through Canvas.

**Bump-up policy**: I reserve the right to "bump up" the grades of students who have made valuable contributions to the course in our in-person classes and labs. This also applies to students who show tremendous progress and growth over the quarter.

## Course policies

**Be nice. Be honest. Don't cheat.**

We will also follow UCI's [Code of Conduct](https://www.compliance.uci.edu/ethical-values.php).

### Attendance and participation

Attendance and participation are important to your success in this course. You are expected to come to *all classes* prepared—having done the reading—and ready to discuss the content. You are also expected to attend *your own lab* every Friday.

Missing a class or lab has the potential to put you significantly behind. Still, life happens. That's why three labs drop from your grade, and you don't need to contact me if you miss one (except for the exams).

If you are sick, hunker down and focus on getting better! Please do not come to class. If you have to miss an exam due to such an unavoidable health or emergency situation, you should message me before the exam starts. Similarly, if you have to miss an exam due to religious reasons, please message me before it starts.

You are expected to arrive before the start of each class to allow us to begin on time.

If you have to miss the midterm exam, you will need to take a similar make-up exam during UCI's final exam period (I would assign a date and time). If at all possible, try to avoid this. There are at least three reasons. First, I deliberately scheduled the midterm exam during a period in which you do not have to worry about other exams—in turn, taking yet another exam during finals week can be stressful. Second, the make-up exam may also include the additional content we will have covered after the midterm. Third, the midterm exam is meant to prepare you for the remainder of our course—you would miss an important opportunity to check your knowledge.

### Staying focused during class

Let's stay focused!

Evidence from multiple randomized experiments indicates that students who take notes on their laptops or tablets learn less than those who take notes using pen/pencil and paper. They are also more likely to adversely affect their peers' learning and grades (see Prof. Susan M. Dynarski's [summary of the evidence](http://brook.gs/2vS6I3e)). Therefore, while not prohibited, using a laptop or tablet is strongly discouraged during lectures.

There are only three exceptions:

1. I may prompt you to take out your laptop or phone (e.g., to answer a poll).
2. You may use a tablet that lays flat on your table, with a stylus pen (i.e., without typing on a keyboard).
3. You have an [accommodation plan](https://dsc.uci.edu/accommodations/) requiring a tablet or laptop.

Cell phone use is prohibited during class (unless I ask you to take out your phone). Please stow your phone away. In our Friday labs, you'll use a laptop for the spreadsheet and the simulator.

### Late assignments

You should budget enough time to submit all assignments well ahead of each deadline (Sunday, 6 PM). A one-day extension is granted automatically, to cover holidays, sickness, or any other reasons (Monday, 6 PM).

No questions asked.

I suggest using the extension cautiously, though, just in case something happens, you get sick, or any other issue arises that keeps you from submitting your homework on time. Late assignments past the extension will not be accepted, regardless of how late they are. On top of the extension, I disregard your lowest Mastery Training and your lowest Problem Set.

### Academic honesty

Violation of the [UCI Academic Senate Policy on Academic Integrity](https://conduct.uci.edu/academic-integrity/) will result in an F in the course and possible disciplinary action. Violating the Academic Integrity Policy is unacceptable, devaluing the teaching and learning experience for the entire community.

You're welcome to use AI to learn: to explain an idea, make practice problems, or help with a spreadsheet formula. Don't use it to get answers to MindTap questions. Homework is your practice for the exams and quizzes, where you'll have no AI and no devices. AI also makes mistakes in statistics, so check what it tells you.

### Recordings

I will not record our in-person classes. Also, you are not allowed to record the class, unless you have an [accommodation plan](https://dsc.uci.edu/accommodations/) that requires a recording.

### Drop policy

Following [UCI's policy](https://www.reg.uci.edu/enrollment/adc/adcpolicy.html), drops after the second week of instruction need the dean's approval.

## Doing well

### A personal note

If you tell me you're having trouble, I will not judge you or think less of you. I hope you'll extend me the same grace.

You *never* owe me personal information about your health (mental or physical). You are *always* welcome to talk to me about things that you're going through, though. If I can't help you, I usually know somebody who can.

If you need extra help, or if you feel like you're behind or not understanding everything, **do not suffer in silence.** Talk to me! I will work with you.

### Student hours

Please watch this video:

<div class="ratio ratio-16x9" style="max-width: 640px; margin: 0 auto 1rem;">
<iframe title="Video: What are Office Hours? by Andrew Ishak" src="https://player.vimeo.com/video/270014784" frameborder="0" allow="autoplay; fullscreen" allowfullscreen></iframe>

Student hours are set times dedicated to all of you (most professors call these "office hours"; I don't).[^studenthours] This means that I will be waiting for you to come by to talk to me---either remotely or in-person---with whatever questions you have. This is the best and easiest way to find me and the best chance for discussing class material and concerns.

[^studenthours]: There's fairly widespread misunderstanding about what office hours actually are! [Many students often think that they are the times I *shouldn't* be disturbed](https://www.chronicle.com/article/Can-This-Man-Change-How-Elite/245714/), which is the exact opposite of what they're for!

It is easiest to meet with me online. [Make an appointment with me here]({{< var instructor.appointment_url >}})—the confirmation e-mail will contain a link for a Zoom meeting (the default). If you prefer an in-person meeting, (1) schedule a Zoom meeting first, then (2) contact me via e-mail, at least one day before our meeting.

{{< var assistant.name_no_title >}} also holds drop-in student hours. She'll share the times in the first lab.

### On-campus resources

Life at UCI can be complicated and challenging. Fortunately, UCI offers a wealth of resources to support you.

Please take the time to seriously consider the following (confidential) resources available to you.

- [Emergency food and toiletries](https://basicneeds.uci.edu/fresh-pantry/)
- [More broadly, services at the UCI Basic Needs Center](https://basicneeds.uci.edu/all-services/)
- [Services at the UCI Counseling Center](https://counseling.uci.edu)
- [Support to become a better writer](http://www.writingcenter.uci.edu)
- [Guides at UCI Libraries](https://guides.lib.uci.edu/), including on [academic writing](https://guides.lib.uci.edu/scientificwriting) and how to [cite your sources](https://guides.lib.uci.edu/citations)
- [Tutoring and mentoring options](https://larc.uci.edu/all-services/)
- [Resources at UCI's Cross-Cultural Center](https://ccc.uci.edu)
- [Resources for DACA students](https://ssi.uci.edu/dreamscholars/)
- [Resources for first-generation college students](http://firstgen.due.uci.edu)
- [Resources for those caring for (or expecting) little anteaters](https://ssi.uci.edu/spf/)

One of the (very few) things I regret from college is that I did not ask for enough help. I'm sure at least one of the above can help you do better---do reach out.

### Safety

**I will listen to and believe you if someone is threatening you.**

If you are in immediate danger, call 911. UCI police provides a safety escort (949-824-7233) and a 24-hour *non*-emergency line (949-824-5223). Save these numbers.

Please double-check and make sure you are signed up to [zotAlert](https://www.oit.uci.edu/services/communication-collaboration/zotalert/).

If you are experiencing sexual assault or misconduct, domestic or relationship violence, stalking, or retaliation, please report it to me and I will connect you to resources. The University of California, Irvine is committed to creating and maintaining an environment in which all persons who live, work, and learn in our campus community can be free of sexual assault, sexual misconduct, relationship violence, stalking, and retaliation. Every member of the University community should be aware that sexual violence is prohibited by law as well as our University policy and will not be tolerated.

At any time---even if you are in doubt, or would like to know more about what you can do to *prevent* cases---do not hesitate to reach out to [UCI Care](https://care.uci.edu/) and the [Sexual Harassment/Title IX Officer (SHO)](https://www.oeod.uci.edu/sho/index.php).

### Accommodations and accessibility

If you wish to request academic accommodations you may do so through the [Disability Services Center (DSC)](https://dsc.uci.edu/accommodations/). To obtain services, please [register with DSC](https://dsc.uci.edu/register/) and complete the [DSC Intake Form](https://uci-accommodate.symplicity.com). You should then make an appointment with me during the first week of class to discuss any accommodations that need to be made.

At the University of California, Irvine, providing a culture of inclusion and equal opportunity for students with disabilities is a campuswide responsibility and commitment. If you have difficulty accessing any materials for this course, please let me know by email at <a href='mailto:{{< var instructor.email >}}'>{{< var instructor.email >}}</a> as soon as possible.

I will do everything possible to make sure our course materials are accessible. My slides come in two versions: an HTML version, which works with screen readers (including the math) and lets you zoom, and a PDF version for printing. *Please* let me know if you know of ways to improve on this further. Even a short message on, say, the colors I use on a slide can help a lot.
